## Source: AGENTS.md

# Agent guide

## Project and scope

This repository builds and documents a custom x86-64 WSL2 kernel profile for
eBPF observability and networking. It contains Bash/Python tooling, a kernel
configuration fragment, Compose examples, and GitHub Actions workflows. It does
not implement Linux, Tetragon, Cilium, Envoy, or OBI themselves.

Start with [the repository map](docs/REPOSITORY_MAP.md) and [README.md](README.md).
Use [llms.txt](llms.txt) as the navigation index. [llms-full.txt](llms-full.txt)
is a generated documentation bundle for consumers that prefer one input file.
Source files remain authoritative when prose and implementation disagree.

## Browsing and indexing

- Search this project's `scripts/`, `tests/`, `examples/`, `.github/workflows/`,
  root documentation, and configuration first.
- Treat `WSL2-Linux-Kernel/` as vendored upstream source. Exclude it from default
  repository indexing and broad searches; inspect specific upstream files only
  when a kernel dependency or behavior needs verification.
- Exclude `.git/`, Python caches, the local `examples/.env`, kernel build output,
  modules/VHDX images, and `kernel-release.txt` from knowledge indexes.
- Index individual documentation pages or `llms-full.txt`, rather than both,
  when duplicate text would impair retrieval.
- Relative links in `llms.txt` resolve against the checked-out repository or
  the URL serving that file. These files guide browsing; they do not force a
  crawler to index the repository or enforce access restrictions.

## Source and update invariants

- Keep the kernel submodule gitlink and `KERNEL_COMMIT` in `kernel-version.env`
  identical. `KERNEL_TAG` must resolve to that commit.
- Keep the repository URL and tracking series consistent between `.gitmodules`
  and the source lock. The scheduled updater stays in the current stable series.
- Initialize with `scripts/prepare-kernel.sh`; ordinary builds must use the
  committed pin, not `git submodule update --remote`.
- Preserve local source/configuration changes. Review `git status --short`
  before edits and do not reset a dirty submodule to make validation pass.
- Keep changes to upstream kernel files separate from this repository's tooling.
  A kernel-series upgrade requires review of symbols, packaging, and runtime
  compatibility; it is not an automatic weekly bump.

## Kernel configuration

- Add desired options to `ebpf-kernel.config`; do not edit Microsoft's tracked
  base config. Add missing parent dependencies instead of weakening the validator.
- `scripts/configure-kernel.sh` starts from the pinned Microsoft base, merges the
  fragment, appends `bpf` to the existing LSM order, resolves Kconfig, and checks
  all requested values. Preserve the other LSMs when changing this flow.
- `CONFIG_BPF_LSM=y` alone does not activate BPF LSM. Runtime activation also
  depends on the LSM list and any `lsm=` command-line override.
- Tetragon's kprobe `Override` requires `FUNCTION_ERROR_INJECTION` and
  `BPF_KPROBE_OVERRIDE`. These requirements differ from ordinary observation.
- Keep the custom local-version suffix so the runtime check can distinguish
  this profile from the managed Microsoft kernel.

## Validation and environments

Run lightweight checks from the repository root:

```bash
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v
python3 scripts/build-llms.py --check
python3 scripts/check-links.py
for script in scripts/*.sh; do bash -n "$script"; done
```

`scripts/validate-repository.sh` additionally needs ShellCheck and Docker Compose
v2. Compose parsing does not require a running Docker daemon. Use Actionlint for
workflow changes when available. Tests use Python's standard-library `unittest`;
no Python package installation is needed for the tooling.

Kernel configuration/builds require x86-64 Linux and the prerequisites in the
README. Use a case-sensitive Linux filesystem. macOS and Windows host filesystems
may collapse distinct upstream kernel filenames and create apparent source
changes. Hosted Linux CI validates Kconfig resolution, not a full kernel build.

Only claim checks that were actually executed. Distinguish static/lint/unit
checks, Linux configuration resolution, full compilation, WSL boot, runtime BPF
probes, and application smoke tests. Follow the README's rollback and runtime
verification procedures when testing on Windows/WSL.

## Workflows and containers

The scheduled update workflow creates/refreshes
`automation/update-wsl-kernel` and an update PR after configuration validation.
It never merges automatically. Keep no-op discovery lightweight, preserve an
identical pending commit, and retain the explicit force-with-lease check for
changed managed branches. The repository's default workflow token remains
read-only; the update job requests contents and pull-request writes, while the release draft
job requests contents writes. Release builds request OIDC and attestation writes,
keep contents read-only, and create drafts
for Windows acceptance testing before publication. Preserve fail-closed verification
of immutable assets and provenance against the fixed repository, workflow, and tag.

The Compose example targets Docker Engine inside the WSL distro. Docker Desktop
has a separate daemon environment; do not imply that a user-distro mount or PID
namespace automatically reaches Desktop workloads. Keep broad agent privileges
and relaxed sandbox profiles explicit in documentation.

## Documentation maintenance

Update the README and repository map when entry points or workflow behavior
change. `llms.txt` is the small, curated index; keep it useful without embedding
the full upstream kernel tree. After changing documentation, regenerate the
bundle and verify it:

```bash
python3 scripts/build-llms.py
python3 scripts/build-llms.py --check
```

Do not edit `llms-full.txt` directly. The generator includes a bounded allowlist
of project documentation, normalizes local links, and excludes vendored source,
build artifacts, and local environment files.

## Source: docs/REPOSITORY_MAP.md

# Repository map

This project supplies a WSL2 kernel configuration/build guide and supporting
tooling. It has no application server or persistent data store. Bash orchestrates
Git and Kconfig; Python validates configuration and chooses upstream release tags.

## Read first

- [Agent instructions](AGENTS.md): scope, indexing boundaries, invariants, and checks.
- [Installation and runtime guide](README.md): the complete WSL setup and rollback flow.
- [Kernel option explanations](KERNEL_CONFIG_EXPLAINED.md): the requested profile and dependencies.
- [Source lock](kernel-version.env): current release tag, upstream URL, and immutable commit.

## File responsibilities

| Path | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| `.gitmodules`, `WSL2-Linux-Kernel/` | Registered Microsoft kernel submodule; the gitlink is the build's source pin |
| `kernel-version.env` | Human-readable release/commit lock checked against the gitlink |
| `ebpf-kernel.config` | Requested built-in eBPF, tracing, network, storage, and enforcement options |
| `scripts/build-release.sh` | Compile and package binaries, checksums, metadata, and exact source archives |
| `scripts/Install-WslEbpfKernel.ps1` | Verify immutable assets and signed provenance for an explicit tag; back up and merge Windows settings |
| `.github/workflows/release.yml` | Pinned Actions, version-tag build, provenance attestation, and draft release publication |
| `scripts/prepare-kernel.sh` | Check lock/gitlink agreement and initialize the pinned submodule |
| `scripts/configure-kernel.sh` | Back up `.config`, merge the fragment, preserve LSMs, resolve dependencies |
| `scripts/check-config.py` | Fail on missing/changed options, invalid input, or absent BPF LSM activation |
| `scripts/verify-runtime.sh` | Compare the running release; check BTF, mounts, LSMs, BPF probes, optional Tetragon probes |
| `scripts/update-kernel.py` | Discover stable tags in the pinned series and stage a verified submodule/lock update |
| `scripts/write-update-pr-body.py` | Render the kernel-update PR description from release and GitHub run metadata |
| `scripts/validate-repository.sh` | Run lint, link/bundle checks, unit tests, and Compose parsing |
| `scripts/check-links.py` | Validate local links in project docs and LLM navigation files |
| `scripts/build-llms.py` | Generate or check the combined documentation bundle |
| `tests/` | Standard-library Python tests for config parsing/requirements and release selection |
| `examples/compose.yaml`, `examples/.env.example` | Versioned OBI agent and optional HTTP smoke target |
| `.github/dependabot.yml` | Weekly grouped updates for SHA-pinned GitHub Actions |
| `.github/workflows/validate.yml` | Repository checks and pinned-kernel Kconfig resolution on Linux |
| `.github/workflows/update-kernel.yml` | Weekly/manual discovery, candidate validation, managed branch, update PR |
| `llms.txt`, `llms-full.txt` | Curated navigation index and generated documentation bundle |

The source directory may be uninitialized until `scripts/prepare-kernel.sh` runs.
Do not treat its absence as an application source-code gap.

## Build and verification flow

```text
Git submodule pin + source lock
  -> prepare-kernel.sh verifies and initializes source
  -> configure-kernel.sh merges Microsoft base + ebpf-kernel.config
  -> preserve existing CONFIG_LSM, append bpf
  -> olddefconfig resolves dependencies
  -> check-config.py verifies requested values
  -> README build commands compile kernel and package modules.vhdx
  -> Windows .wslconfig selects artifacts
  -> verify-runtime.sh probes the running WSL kernel
  -> OBI / Tetragon / Cilium workload-specific smoke tests
```

The PowerShell installer downloads published versioned artifacts and updates
`.wslconfig` with a backup. The release workflow creates drafts for manual Windows
acceptance testing before publication. Kernel support
does not install the agents or prove a particular enforcement/networking policy.

## Upstream update flow

The update workflow checks release metadata before downloading source. If a newer
stable tag exists in the current major/minor series, it initializes the existing
pin, fetches and verifies the new tag's commit, then stages both the gitlink and
source lock. Repository checks and Linux Kconfig resolution must pass before it
publishes `automation/update-wsl-kernel` and opens/refreshes a PR.

Numeric comparison avoids lexicographic tag ordering. Annotated tags use their
peeled commit. Prereleases and different series are excluded. A missing/moved
current tag fails for manual investigation. Identical pending trees retain their
existing commit; changed trees use an explicit lease when updating the managed
branch. A maintainer reviews and merges; Windows boot and workload validation
remain separate acceptance checks.

## Where to investigate a problem

| Symptom | Start here |
|---|---|
| Fresh clone cannot fetch/initialize the kernel | `.gitmodules`, source lock, `prepare-kernel.sh` |
| An option disappears or becomes modular | Fragment, `check-config.py`, and the exact pinned upstream Kconfig dependency |
| BPF LSM compiled but unavailable | `configure-kernel.sh`, active LSM list, Windows `lsm=` override |
| OBI cannot observe another process/container | Compose capabilities, daemon host, host PID namespace, mount types |
| Updater selects an unexpected release | `select_release` in `update-kernel.py` and `tests/test_update_kernel.py` |
| CI fails | The failing workflow step, then the corresponding script; do not weaken checks to hide a dependency |
| Agent index is too large or duplicated | Exclude the upstream submodule/artifacts; choose individual docs or the full bundle |

## Indexing boundaries

Index first-party scripts, tests, workflows, examples, root configuration, and
documentation. Exclude the upstream kernel tree from default indexing, and fetch
specific upstream paths at the source-lock commit when needed. Exclude Git
metadata, caches, compiled kernel/modules, VHDX images, and the local `.env`.

`llms.txt` and `AGENTS.md` are guidance and navigation, not crawler enforcement.
The full bundle is generated from a fixed documentation allowlist; use the
source pages when exact implementation behavior matters.

## Evidence

- [Source initialization](scripts/prepare-kernel.sh)
- [Kernel configuration](scripts/configure-kernel.sh)

- [Update PR description](scripts/write-update-pr-body.py)
- [Validation workflow](.github/workflows/validate.yml)
- [Scheduled update workflow](.github/workflows/update-kernel.yml)

## Source: README.md

# Enabling eBPF in WSL2 — Custom Kernel for Tetragon & OTel OBI

Build a reproducible x86-64 WSL2 kernel profile for Docker Engine, Tetragon,
Cilium, OpenTelemetry OBI, and transparent proxy workloads. Microsoft's kernel
already enables much of the required eBPF functionality, including BTF and
kprobes. First inspect your running kernel: a custom build is useful when you
need missing features, such as Tetragon's kprobe return override, BPF LSM
activation, or sockmap support.

The [configuration fragment](ebpf-kernel.config) pins this project's requested
profile. [KERNEL_CONFIG_EXPLAINED.md](KERNEL_CONFIG_EXPLAINED.md) explains the
options. Kernel support alone does not install or configure these applications.

For repository navigation and indexing, start with [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md),
[the repository map](docs/REPOSITORY_MAP.md), or [llms.txt](llms.txt). A generated
[full documentation bundle](llms-full.txt) is available for single-file ingestion.
These guides keep the upstream kernel tree and local build artifacts outside
the default project index.

## Scope and verification status

| Component | Baseline / status |
|---|---|
| Architecture | x86-64 only; ARM64 needs its own config, image path, and validation |
| Build environment | Ubuntu 24.04 on x86-64 Linux / WSL2; configuration CI uses Ubuntu 24.04 |
| Kernel source | Git submodule pinned to the release and commit in [kernel-version.env](kernel-version.env) |
| WSL | WSL2 with support for `.wslconfig` `kernel` and `kernelModules`; inspect `wsl --version` |
| Docker example | Docker Engine inside the same WSL distro; Compose v2 |
| OBI example | Versioned image selected in [examples/.env.example](examples/.env.example) |
| Automated checks | Script syntax, validator regressions, local links, Compose parsing, and Linux Kconfig resolution |
| Windows boot and workload tests | Require the runtime and smoke checks below; CI does not boot WSL |

The source pin is a reproducibility baseline, not a claim that this is the newest
or recommended security release. Review Microsoft's supported releases when
maintaining your installation. Update both entries in
[kernel-version.env](kernel-version.env) and the submodule commit together, then
repeat configuration, boot, and workload validation. Do not follow a moving upstream branch: different
kernel series can change configuration symbols and module packaging scripts.

## Install a prebuilt release

Published [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/knightfall/WSL2-enable-eBPF/releases)
provide an x86-64 `bzImage`, matching `modules.vhdx`, resolved configuration,
SHA-256 checksums, build metadata, runtime verifier, exact source archives, and
a portable Sigstore build-provenance bundle.
A release is available only after a maintainer publishes its draft.

Install [GitHub CLI](https://cli.github.com/) separately and authenticate using
`gh auth login`. Use a current version supporting `release verify`,
`release verify-asset`, and the attestation policy flags below. Download the
installer and evidence with GitHub CLI. **Verify the installer before executing
it**, using this PowerShell sequence and your actual published release tag:

```powershell
$tag = 'ebpf-v1.0.0'
$repo = 'knightfall/WSL2-enable-eBPF'
gh release download $tag --repo $repo --pattern Install-WslEbpfKernel.ps1 --pattern provenance.sigstore.json
if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Download failed' }
gh release verify $tag --repo $repo
if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Release verification failed' }
gh release verify-asset $tag ./Install-WslEbpfKernel.ps1 --repo $repo
if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Installer release verification failed' }
gh attestation verify ./Install-WslEbpfKernel.ps1 --repo $repo --bundle ./provenance.sigstore.json --signer-workflow "$repo/.github/workflows/release.yml" --source-ref "refs/tags/$tag" --deny-self-hosted-runners
if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Installer provenance verification failed' }
```

Then inspect and run the verified installer:

```powershell
.\Install-WslEbpfKernel.ps1 -ReleaseTag ebpf-v1.0.0 -WhatIf
.\Install-WslEbpfKernel.ps1 -ReleaseTag ebpf-v1.0.0
```

The installer uses GitHub CLI to download that explicit version, verifies release
immutability, verifies the checksum manifest's signed build provenance, and checks
each kernel, module image, release identifier, and verifier against both the
release attestation and build provenance before checking `SHA256SUMS`. It installs into
`%USERPROFILE%\wsl-kernel\<tag>`, and backs up `.wslconfig` before changing only
`kernel` and `kernelModules` in `[wsl2]`. It preserves other settings, rejects
duplicate sections and existing `lsm=` overrides, and refuses to overwrite an
existing release directory. It checks the native processor architecture, so
ARM64 hosts running emulated x64 PowerShell are rejected. If copying assets or
writing configuration fails, it removes the release directory created by that
attempt so the same version can be retried; existing installations are preserved.
Verification pins the repository identity, `.github/workflows/release.yml`, and
`refs/tags/<requested-tag>`, and rejects self-hosted-runner attestations. Any
verification or download failure stops installation before configuration changes.
There is no bypass switch. The evidence bundle is saved with the installed files.

This establishes origin and integrity within the trusted GitHub Actions/Sigstore
system, not absence of vulnerabilities or independent reproducibility. Public
repository attestations have public transparency-log evidence; private repository
attestations use GitHub's separate Sigstore instance without a public log. See
[GitHub's trust model](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/security/artifact-attestations).
The unsigned verification bundle is itself verified as an immutable release
asset; its embedded signatures are validated against GitHub CLI's trusted roots.

These settings apply to **all WSL2 distributions**. The installer does not stop
running workloads. When ready, run `wsl --shutdown`, start WSL, and follow
section 7 for mounts, BPF probes, and workload checks. The installer saves
`kernel-release.txt` and `ebpf-kernel.config` alongside the binaries, and
`scripts/verify-runtime.sh` plus `scripts/check-config.py` beneath the release
directory. Both scripts and the fragment are authenticated before installation.
After mounting the filesystems in section 7, use the installed verifier from WSL
without cloning this repository:

```bash
WIN_PROFILE=$(powershell.exe -NoProfile -Command '[Console]::Write($env:USERPROFILE)' | tr -d '\r\n')
RELEASE_DIR="$(wslpath -u "$WIN_PROFILE")/wsl-kernel/ebpf-v1.0.0"
sudo bash "$RELEASE_DIR/scripts/verify-runtime.sh" "$(cat "$RELEASE_DIR/kernel-release.txt")"
```

Substitute your installed tag. The runtime prerequisites in section 7, including
`python3` and a working `bpftool`, still apply. Follow section 6 for
access-denied troubleshooting and rollback. Custom kernels require manual updates.

### Publish a release

Before tagging, enable **Settings → General → Releases → Enable release
immutability**. This affects future published releases; drafts remain editable.
The installer requires immutable releases and rejects mutable ones. See
[release immutability](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/concepts/supply-chain-security/immutable-releases).
GitHub artifact attestations require a public repository on Free/Pro/Team, or
GitHub Enterprise Cloud for private repositories. Confirm eligibility before
building a release; the workflow never silently falls back to checksums. See
[attestation availability](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/secure-your-work/use-artifact-attestations/use-artifact-attestations).
Restrict creation of `ebpf-v*` tags to maintainers with a repository ruleset.

Commit the build tooling and reviewed source pin, then push a version tag such
as `ebpf-v1.0.0`. [The release workflow](.github/workflows/release.yml) validates
the repository, compiles the pinned kernel on Ubuntu 24.04, packages modules
using Microsoft's script, attests every packaged object (including the installer, checksums, and source),
and creates a **draft** release with the evidence bundle. The build job has
`id-token: write` and `attestations: write`; only the draft job has
`contents: write`. Release workflow Actions are pinned to immutable commits. The build timeout is three hours; large
source archives and kernel builds may require a larger runner if hosted limits
are reached. Use a fresh x86-64 Linux checkout for local packaging:

```bash
./scripts/build-release.sh
```

The `dist/` directory contains the assets. `kernel-source.tar.xz` contains the
exact upstream tree and licenses; `build-source.tar.xz` contains this repository's
committed tooling and fragment. Keep both available with the binaries. The build
records the repository commit and upstream pin, but is not claimed bit-for-bit
reproducible across toolchains.

Before publishing the draft, test its exact binary assets on Windows: boot,
module loading, runtime BPF probes, relevant workload smoke tests, and rollback.
During draft acceptance, download assets with authenticated GitHub CLI and
verify their build attestations with the policy above; immutable release
verification becomes available at publication. Configure the test machine
manually using sections 5–6, since the installer intentionally rejects drafts.
Update the release notes with evidence, then publish through GitHub. Publication
locks the assets and tag and creates GitHub's release attestation. Afterwards,
verify the published installer and exercise its normal installation flow.
Configuration validation and successful compilation alone do not prove WSL boot.
No tag or release is created by a local build.

## 1. Check the environment and install prerequisites

In Windows PowerShell:

```powershell
wsl --version
wsl --list --verbose
```

Confirm the build distro uses WSL version 2. Inside that distro:

```bash
uname -m # these instructions require x86_64
sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y git build-essential flex bison dwarves libssl-dev libelf-dev \
  cpio qemu-utils rsync python3 xz-utils bc libncurses-dev
pahole --version
```

`dwarves` supplies `pahole` for BTF generation. The detected version depends on
your installed package; it need not be exactly 1.25. `libncurses-dev` is used by
the optional `menuconfig` interface. Build on the distro's Linux filesystem
(for example, under `$HOME`), rather than a Windows `/mnt/c` directory.

## 2. Fetch the pinned kernel source

```bash
git clone https://github.com/knightfall/WSL2-enable-eBPF.git
cd WSL2-enable-eBPF
REPO_DIR="$PWD"
./scripts/prepare-kernel.sh
KERNEL_DIR="$REPO_DIR/WSL2-Linux-Kernel"
```

The setup script checks that the Git submodule commit and source lock agree,
then initializes the kernel at that exact commit. Local changes in an existing
submodule are rejected and preserved. You can also initialize a fresh clone with
`git submodule update --init --depth 1`; do not use `--remote` for ordinary builds,
because it bypasses the committed source pin.

The remaining Linux commands assume the same shell and the variables above.
After opening a new shell, set `REPO_DIR` to the absolute path of this repository
and `KERNEL_DIR` to its nested kernel checkout.

## 3. Configure and validate the kernel

```bash
"$REPO_DIR/scripts/configure-kernel.sh" "$KERNEL_DIR"
```

This backs up any previous `.config`, starts from `Microsoft/config-wsl`, merges
`ebpf-kernel.config`, preserves Microsoft's LSM list and appends `bpf`, then runs
`olddefconfig`. The validator fails if any requested value is missing, disabled,
or changed by dependency resolution. It also checks that `CONFIG_LSM` contains
`bpf`. The fragment enables `CONFIG_FUNCTION_ERROR_INJECTION` and
`CONFIG_BPF_KPROBE_OVERRIDE` for Tetragon policies using kprobe `Override` actions.

Optional interactive changes must be followed by validation:

```bash
cd "$KERNEL_DIR"
make menuconfig KCONFIG_CONFIG=.config
make olddefconfig KCONFIG_CONFIG=.config
python3 "$REPO_DIR/scripts/check-config.py" .config
grep '^CONFIG_PAHOLE_VERSION=' .config
```

If BTF configuration fails, check `pahole --version` and the Kconfig dependency
messages, then rerun configuration. Setting `CONFIG_DEBUG_INFO=y` alone cannot
select a debug-information format; Microsoft's base config supplies that choice.
Keep module BTF mismatch disabled so incompatible module BTF does not get
silently accepted.

## 4. Build and package modules

```bash
cd "$KERNEL_DIR"
# JOBS can be reduced when the WSL VM has limited memory.
make -j"${JOBS:-$(nproc)}" KCONFIG_CONFIG=.config
make KCONFIG_CONFIG=.config INSTALL_MOD_PATH="$KERNEL_DIR/modules" modules_install
make -s KCONFIG_CONFIG=.config kernelrelease > "$REPO_DIR/kernel-release.txt"

sudo ./Microsoft/scripts/gen_modules_vhdx.sh \
  "$KERNEL_DIR/modules" \
  "$(cat "$REPO_DIR/kernel-release.txt")" \
  "$KERNEL_DIR/modules.vhdx"
```

`make clean` preserves `.config`; `make mrproper` removes it. If you change the
source pin, use a fresh source checkout and module staging directory so stale
artifacts cannot be included. The packaging command above belongs to the pinned
6.6 source series; check upstream instructions when changing kernel series.

## 5. Copy artifacts and preserve a rollback path

In PowerShell, back up your existing global WSL settings before editing:

```powershell
$configPath = Join-Path $env:USERPROFILE '.wslconfig'
if (Test-Path $configPath) {
    Copy-Item $configPath "$configPath.backup-$(Get-Date -Format yyyyMMdd-HHmmss)"
}
```

Inside the WSL build shell, obtain the actual Windows profile path. A profile
directory is not necessarily `C:\Users\<USERNAME>`:

```bash
WIN_PROFILE=$(powershell.exe -NoProfile -Command '[Console]::Write($env:USERPROFILE)' | tr -d '\r\n')
test -n "$WIN_PROFILE"
WIN_KERNEL_DIR="$(wslpath -u "$WIN_PROFILE")/wsl-kernel/$(cat "$REPO_DIR/kernel-release.txt")-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)"
mkdir -p "$WIN_KERNEL_DIR"
cp "$KERNEL_DIR/arch/x86/boot/bzImage" "$WIN_KERNEL_DIR/bzImage"
cp "$KERNEL_DIR/modules.vhdx" "$WIN_KERNEL_DIR/modules.vhdx"
wslpath -w "$WIN_KERNEL_DIR/bzImage"
wslpath -w "$WIN_KERNEL_DIR/modules.vhdx"
```

Use a new release directory for each installation and retain the previous
artifacts until the new kernel passes runtime checks.

## 6. Configure Windows WSL

In PowerShell:

```powershell
notepad "$env:USERPROFILE\.wslconfig"
```

Add or update these keys in the existing `[wsl2]` section. Substitute the paths
printed above, doubling each backslash as shown. Use literal paths:

```ini
[wsl2]
kernel=C:\\Users\\YOUR-PROFILE\\wsl-kernel\\YOUR-INSTALL-DIRECTORY\\bzImage
kernelModules=C:\\Users\\YOUR-PROFILE\\wsl-kernel\\YOUR-INSTALL-DIRECTORY\\modules.vhdx
```

Preserve other settings and avoid duplicate `[wsl2]` sections. These settings
apply globally to WSL2 distributions. If an existing `kernelCommandLine` includes
an `lsm=` argument, it overrides `CONFIG_LSM`; preserve that argument's existing
LSMs and append `bpf`, or remove the override if it is no longer needed.

If Windows reports access denied for either artifact, grant read access to the
virtual-machine group from an Administrator PowerShell session. SID syntax also
works on non-English Windows installations:

```powershell
$kernelDir = Read-Host 'Full Windows path to the release directory created above'
icacls "$kernelDir\bzImage" /grant '*S-1-5-83-0:(R)'
icacls "$kernelDir\modules.vhdx" /grant '*S-1-5-83-0:(R)'
```

Restart WSL from PowerShell:

```powershell
wsl --shutdown
wsl
```

### Roll back if WSL fails to boot

Windows can edit `.wslconfig` even when the Linux distro cannot start. Restore
your saved configuration, or remove only `kernel` and `kernelModules` from
`[wsl2]` to return to Microsoft's managed kernel. If you added an `lsm=` override
for this setup, restore its previous value too. Then run `wsl --shutdown` and
start the distro again. Keep other WSL settings intact.

## 7. Mount filesystems and verify the running kernel

Inside the WSL distro using the custom kernel:

```bash
mountpoint -q /sys/fs/bpf || sudo mount -t bpf bpffs /sys/fs/bpf
mountpoint -q /sys/kernel/tracing || sudo mount -t tracefs tracefs /sys/kernel/tracing
mountpoint -q /sys/kernel/security || sudo mount -t securityfs securityfs /sys/kernel/security
findmnt -T /sys/fs/cgroup # expected: cgroup2
```

To persist mounts, add the following entries to `/etc/fstab` once, preserving
existing entries:

```fstab
bpffs /sys/fs/bpf bpf defaults 0 0
tracefs /sys/kernel/tracing tracefs defaults 0 0
securityfs /sys/kernel/security securityfs defaults 0 0
```

WSL processes `/etc/fstab` when `[automount] mountFsTab=true` in `/etc/wsl.conf`
(the default); systemd is not required for that mechanism. If you use systemd to
run Docker Engine, enable it separately:

```ini
# /etc/wsl.conf — merge into any existing [boot] section
[boot]
systemd=true
```

After changing `wsl.conf`, restart with `wsl --shutdown` from Windows. Install
`bpftool` using a distro package or build it from the pinned kernel's
`tools/bpf/bpftool` source. Some `linux-tools` wrappers require a binary matching
the running kernel, so verify that `bpftool version` actually works.

```bash
sudo "$REPO_DIR/scripts/verify-runtime.sh" "$(cat "$REPO_DIR/kernel-release.txt")"
```

This checks the expected kernel release, embedded configuration, readable kernel
BTF, filesystem types, active BPF LSM, and available BPF program/map types.
It runs Tetragon's probes when `tetra` is installed. Before using enforcement,
install the CLI matching your Tetragon deployment and run:

```bash
tetra probe config
sudo tetra probe
```

Check `override_return` and `lsm` in the probe output, then exercise your actual
policy against a disposable target. A successful kernel probe does not prove a
specific policy, application runtime, or Cilium networking mode works.

## 8. Run OBI with Docker Engine inside WSL

Use Docker Engine running in this distro and mount the host filesystems **before**
starting the agent. Check `docker context show` and `docker info` to confirm which
daemon the CLI uses. The agent needs the daemon host's PID namespace and
filesystems, which may differ from those of the shell running Compose.

The [Compose example](examples/compose.yaml) supplies `pid: host`, the capabilities
used by application instrumentation and context propagation, and host mounts for
bpffs, tracefs, and cgroup v2. It relaxes the agent's AppArmor and seccomp profiles
and grants broad `SYS_ADMIN` access; review and narrow permissions for your
selected OBI features using the official capability guide. It fails early when
required capabilities are absent. Mounting existing bpffs before startup makes
pinned maps visible through a normal bind; shared propagation is unnecessary for
this example.

```bash
cd "$REPO_DIR"
cp examples/.env.example examples/.env
docker compose --env-file examples/.env -f examples/compose.yaml config --quiet
docker compose --env-file examples/.env -f examples/compose.yaml --profile demo up -d
curl http://localhost:18080/
docker compose --env-file examples/.env -f examples/compose.yaml logs obi
```

Repeat the request after the agent finishes attaching. Confirm the logs contain
an HTTP trace for the demo server. The example prints traces locally; configure
an OTLP exporter separately when you want to send telemetry to a Collector.
Clean up the smoke workload with:

```bash
docker compose --env-file examples/.env -f examples/compose.yaml --profile demo down
```

To observe your own application, omit `--profile demo` and set `SERVICE_PORT` to
the target process's listening port inside its container. Select the appropriate
versioned OBI image in `examples/.env`. The base example leaves context
propagation at OBI's default; enable it deliberately and test requests between
your services. The tracefs and cgroup mounts are already supplied for modes that
need them. Log enrichment and profile correlation have their own application
and OBI configuration requirements; mounting bpffs alone does not enable them.

### Docker Desktop

Docker Desktop runs its daemon in a separate environment. Do not assume that
mounting bpffs in a user distro mounts it on Desktop's daemon host, or that
`pid: host` refers to that user distro's processes. Docker explicitly documents
that mount propagation does not work with Desktop. The example above targets
Docker Engine inside WSL; Desktop needs separate validation for the precise
version, daemon mounts, and target-process visibility. `privileged: true` does
not correct a namespace or filesystem mismatch.

## Maintenance and local checks

A custom `kernel=` setting bypasses Microsoft's managed kernel selection.
Rebuild and repeat runtime and workload checks when updating the source pin.
Cilium feature requirements vary by routing, encryption, and device mode; for
example, the 6.6 baseline cannot supply features requiring kernel 6.8 or newer.

```bash
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v
python3 scripts/build-llms.py --check
python3 scripts/check-links.py
for script in scripts/*.sh; do bash -n "$script"; done
```

After editing documentation, run `python3 scripts/build-llms.py` to regenerate
the bundle. CI checks for stale bundle content and broken local navigation links. Validation
runs for pull requests and pushes to `main`, cancelling superseded runs for the
same ref. All Actions in the workflows use full commit SHA pins with release
version comments. Dependabot proposes grouped weekly Actions updates; review and
merge those updates to keep the pins current. Validation/build checkouts do not
persist Git credentials; the upstream updater retains credentials for its
managed branch push. Artifacts have bounded retention and missing files fail
uploads; release artifact downloads fail on digest mismatch.

[Configuration CI](.github/workflows/validate.yml) also runs ShellCheck, parses
Compose, fetches the pinned source, merges the fragment, resolves Kconfig on
Linux, and uploads the resulting `.config`. CI success establishes configuration
resolution, not a complete kernel build or WSL boot.

### Scheduled upstream updates

[The upstream update workflow](.github/workflows/update-kernel.yml) runs weekly
on Monday at 03:17 UTC and can be started manually from GitHub Actions. It checks
Microsoft's stable release tags in the currently pinned kernel series (initially
6.6), selects the newest version numerically, and updates both the submodule
gitlink and `kernel-version.env`. New kernel series and prerelease tags are
excluded; changing kernel series requires a separate compatibility review.

When an update exists, the workflow validates the repository and resolves Kconfig
on Linux before pushing the managed `automation/update-wsl-kernel` branch and
opening or refreshing its pull request. It never merges automatically. Unchanged
upstream state avoids downloading the kernel and creates no commit or pull
request. An identical pending update preserves its existing commit and review
state. A moved or missing pinned tag fails the run for manual investigation.

The workflow uses the repository's `GITHUB_TOKEN` with write permissions limited
to its update job. Under **Settings → Actions → General → Workflow permissions**,
allow GitHub Actions to create pull requests; the default token permission can
remain read-only. Pull-request checks created by `GITHUB_TOKEN` may need a
maintainer to approve them. The update run itself validates configuration before
publishing; build, WSL boot, and workload smoke checks remain required before
merging the update. The schedule becomes active only after this workflow is on
the repository's default branch.

For a read-only local update check:

```bash
python3 scripts/update-kernel.py --check
```

- [OBI capabilities](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/zero-code/obi/security/)

## Source: KERNEL_CONFIG_EXPLAINED.md

# WSL2 eBPF Kernel Configuration — Explained

This document explains every option in `ebpf-kernel.config`, grouped by the same sections used in that file.
Each entry covers **what it is**, **why it's needed**, and links to upstream documentation.

This is a requested kernel profile, not a list of features missing from stock
WSL2 or mandatory for every workload. Most options are inherited from Microsoft's
base config. Use `scripts/configure-kernel.sh` to apply the fragment and preserve
the upstream LSM list; use `scripts/check-config.py` to validate the resolved
configuration. The source baseline is recorded in `kernel-version.env`.

---

## Target workloads

| Tool | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Docker** | Container runtime using overlay2 storage, bridge networking, iptables/nftables |
| **Tetragon** | Cilium's runtime security agent — uses kprobes, tracepoints, and BPF-LSM for enforcement |
| **Cilium** | eBPF-native CNI — tc-BPF datapath, conntrack, overlay encapsulation, WireGuard/IPsec; requirements vary by mode |
| **OpenTelemetry OBI** | eBPF-based auto-instrumentation — uprobes, CO-RE, process discovery, and optional context propagation |
| **Envoy** | L7 proxy — optional TPROXY interception; kernel support does not enable application kTLS or sockmap integration |

---

## 1 · Networking baseline

> These are already present in the pinned Microsoft base configuration. The fragment asserts them as part of this profile, and the validator checks that dependency resolution preserves the requested values.

### `CONFIG_INET`
Enables the **IPv4 Internet protocol suite** (TCP, UDP, ICMP, raw sockets) inside the kernel.
Without it, virtually every network-using workload — and many BPF program types — fails to compile or load.
- [Kconfig: CONFIG_INET](https://cateee.net/lkddb/web-lkddb/INET.html)

### `CONFIG_IPV6`
Enables the **IPv6 protocol stack**. Required by Cilium (dual-stack), OBI, and any workload that targets modern cloud networks.
- [Kconfig: CONFIG_IPV6](https://cateee.net/lkddb/web-lkddb/IPV6.html)

### `CONFIG_NETDEVICES`
Gates compilation of all **network device drivers and virtual devices** (veth, tun, bridge, etc.). Without it, container networking and virtual network interfaces cannot exist.
- [Kconfig: CONFIG_NETDEVICES](https://cateee.net/lkddb/web-lkddb/NETDEVICES.html)

### `CONFIG_CRYPTO`
Enables the kernel **crypto API framework** — the substrate used by TLS, IPsec (ESP), WireGuard, and BPF crypto helpers.
- [Kconfig: CONFIG_CRYPTO](https://cateee.net/lkddb/web-lkddb/CRYPTO.html)

### `CONFIG_KEYS`
Provides the **kernel key-retention service** used by keyrings for TLS session keys, IPsec SAs, and module signing.
- [Kconfig: CONFIG_KEYS](https://cateee.net/lkddb/web-lkddb/KEYS.html)

---

## 2 · BTF / CO-RE — required for Tetragon, OBI, Cilium

> **CO-RE** (Compile Once – Run Everywhere) lets a single pre-compiled eBPF binary adapt to any kernel version at load time by reading BTF type information embedded in the kernel image. This eliminates the need to ship a compiler with your eBPF tooling or to recompile code on every target machine.

### `CONFIG_DEBUG_INFO`
Instructs the compiler to embed **DWARF debug information** in kernel objects.
`CONFIG_DEBUG_INFO_BTF` depends on this to generate BTF from the DWARF data via `pahole` (v1.16+, v1.21+ for DWARF 5).
In this kernel series, `DEBUG_INFO` is selected by the debug-information format
choice. Microsoft's base config selects `DEBUG_INFO_DWARF_TOOLCHAIN_DEFAULT`;
writing `CONFIG_DEBUG_INFO=y` alone cannot override a `DEBUG_INFO_NONE` choice.
- [Kernel docs: BTF](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/bpf/btf.html)
- [Medium: Building the Linux kernel with BTF](https://medium.com/@suruti94/building-the-linux-kernel-with-btf-1a617cfb4a24)

### `CONFIG_DEBUG_INFO_BTF`
Generates the **vmlinux BTF blob** — a compact, deduplicated type description of the entire kernel. The standard location is `/sys/kernel/btf/vmlinux`.
This is the cornerstone of CO-RE: tools like `bpftool`, Tetragon, Cilium, and OBI read it at startup to resolve struct offsets without needing kernel headers or source code.
- [Kernel docs: BTF](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/bpf/btf.html)
- [CO-RE reference guide — Andrii Nakryiko](https://nakryiko.com/posts/bpf-core-reference-guide/)
- [BPF CO-RE Portability and Design](https://nakryiko.com/posts/bpf-portability-and-co-re/)
- [BTF Troubleshooting Guide](https://www.virtvps.com/btf-mastering-bpf-troubleshooting-unlocking/)

### `CONFIG_DEBUG_INFO_BTF_MODULES`
Extends BTF coverage to **loadable kernel modules**. Tetragon and OBI hook into subsystems that may live in modules (e.g., `nf_conntrack`, `virtio`, filesystem drivers), so their BTF is needed for CO-RE relocation to work in those paths. Without this, BPF programs may fail to load or relocate on systems with kernel module dependencies.
- [Kernel docs: BTF](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/bpf/btf.html)
- [BCC to libbpf conversion guide — Nakryiko](https://nakryiko.com/posts/bcc-to-libbpf-howto-guide/)

---

## 3 · BPF core

> Most of these are already set by `Microsoft/config-wsl`; they are pinned here to prevent accidental regression when rebasing on a new WSL2 kernel tag. See [eBPF ecosystem progress (eunomia 2025)](https://eunomia.dev/blog/2025/02/12/ebpf-ecosystem-progress-in-20242025-a-technical-deep-dive/) for recent kernel improvements.

### `CONFIG_BPF`
The **BPF interpreter and verifier** core. Every other BPF option depends on this.
- [Kernel docs: BPF](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/bpf/index.html)
- [eBPF.io: Introduction & Community Resources](https://ebpf.io/)

### `CONFIG_BPF_SYSCALL`
Exposes the `bpf(2)` system call to user space, allowing programs to **load, attach, and manage BPF programs and maps**.
Without it, no eBPF tooling can function.
- [man2: bpf(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/bpf.2.html)

### `CONFIG_BPF_JIT`
Enables the **BPF Just-In-Time compiler**. On x86-64 and arm64, BPF bytecode is translated to native machine code at load time, eliminating interpreter overhead. Cilium's data-plane throughput critically depends on JIT being enabled — without it, packet processing is 5–10× slower.
- [Kernel docs: BPF JIT](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/bpf/index.html)
- [Cilium system requirements](https://docs.cilium.io/en/stable/operations/system_requirements/)

### `CONFIG_BPF_JIT_DEFAULT_ON`
Makes the JIT compiler **active by default** without requiring `sysctl net.core.bpf_jit_enable=1`. Ensures JIT is on even before any userspace tuning step runs. Recommended for production deployments.
- [Cilium system requirements](https://docs.cilium.io/en/stable/operations/system_requirements/)
- [How to Tune Kernel Parameters for eBPF Performance](https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-01-07-ebpf-kernel-parameter-tuning/view)

### `CONFIG_BPF_LSM`
Enables **BPF Linux Security Module** hooks (since Linux 5.7). Tetragon uses BPF-LSM to enforce policy decisions (e.g., deny `execve`, restrict file access) directly in the kernel, without a traditional LSM module like SELinux or AppArmor. BPF LSM programs are **privileged, validated at load time, and executed at LSM hook points** to perform runtime checks and access control.
Compilation is only one requirement: `CONFIG_LSM` must include `bpf`, and any
`lsm=` kernel command-line override must also include it. The configuration
script appends `bpf` to Microsoft's existing list. Verify activation with
`cat /sys/kernel/security/lsm` after boot; the list must contain a `bpf` entry.
- [Kernel docs: BPF LSM](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/bpf/bpf_lsm.html)
- [Practical Guide to LSM BPF](https://www.ebpf.top/en/post/lsm_bpf_intro/)
- [Tetragon docs](https://tetragon.io/docs/)
- [Medium: LSM BPF and eBPF Security](https://medium.com/@lumontec/some-freshness-with-linux-security-modules-and-ebpf-676ac363a135)

### `CONFIG_CGROUP_BPF`
Allows **BPF programs to be attached to cgroup hooks** (socket, connect, sendmsg, etc.). Cilium uses these for socket-level load balancing; OBI context-propagation modes can use cgroup socket hooks. This does not by itself enable kernel TLS.
- [Kernel docs: cgroup BPF](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.html)

### `CONFIG_XDP_SOCKETS`
Enables **AF_XDP** — zero-copy packet I/O from userspace via XDP sockets. Used by high-performance network applications and some Cilium XDP offload paths.
- [Kernel docs: AF_XDP](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/networking/af_xdp.html)

### `CONFIG_BPF_STREAM_PARSER`
Enables support for BPF socket stream parsing and sockmap/sk_msg programs. This
profile includes it for applications that use socket redirection. It does not
mean Cilium's normal socket load balancer or an ordinary Envoy deployment uses
sockmap; application integration is required.
- [Kernel docs: sockmap](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/bpf/map_sockmap.html)

### `CONFIG_BPF_EVENTS`
Wires **BPF into the perf-events subsystem**, enabling `BPF_PROG_TYPE_PERF_EVENT` programs and perf ring-buffer output from BPF via `bpf_perf_event_output()`. Used by Tetragon and OBI to stream telemetry to userspace.
- [Kernel docs: BPF perf events](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/bpf/index.html)

---

## 4 · Tracing — Tetragon (kprobes/tracepoints) + OBI (uprobes)

> These configurations enable **kernel instrumentation points** that BPF programs can hook into at runtime. Collectively, they enable low-overhead observability without code modification or recompilation. See [Brendan Gregg's eBPF tracing tools](https://www.brendangregg.com/ebpf.html) and [BPF Performance Tools book](https://www.brendangregg.com/bpf-performance-tools-book.html) for comprehensive observability patterns.

### `CONFIG_FTRACE`
The **Function Tracer framework** — the infrastructure that all kernel tracing facilities build on. Kprobes, tracepoints, and dynamic ftrace hooks all depend on it.
- [Kernel docs: ftrace](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/trace/ftrace.html)
- [Brendan Gregg: Kernel analysis with bpftrace (LWN)](https://lwn.net/Articles/794135/)

### `CONFIG_FUNCTION_TRACER`
Instruments every kernel function with a **5-byte NOP** at entry (on x86) that can be patched at runtime to a call into ftrace. Required by `CONFIG_DYNAMIC_FTRACE` and kprobe trampolines.
- [Kernel docs: ftrace](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/trace/ftrace.html)

### `CONFIG_DYNAMIC_FTRACE`
Enables **runtime patching of ftrace NOP stubs** so only actively traced functions carry overhead. Without this, every function call in the kernel would pay a tracing tax even when no probe is active. Critical for production performance.
- [Kernel docs: ftrace](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/trace/ftrace.html)

### `CONFIG_FTRACE_SYSCALLS`
Creates **dedicated tracepoints for every syscall entry/exit** (`sys_enter_<name>`, `sys_exit_<name>`). Tetragon uses these for low-overhead syscall monitoring without kprobing individual syscall handlers. Enables rich syscall observability with minimal performance impact.
- [Kernel docs: ftrace syscalls](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/trace/ftrace.html)
- [Tetragon: Hook points documentation](https://tetragon.io/docs/concepts/tracing-policy/hooks/)

### `CONFIG_KPROBES`
Enables **kernel probes** — dynamic breakpoints on any kernel instruction address, inserted at runtime without modifying kernel code or rebooting.
Tetragon places kprobes on security-sensitive kernel functions (`security_file_open`, `tcp_connect`, `do_exec`, etc.) to observe and optionally block them. Kprobes incur overhead (trap/INT3 instruction) but can hook anywhere.
- [Kernel docs: kprobes](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/trace/kprobes.html)
- [Tetragon: Hook points documentation](https://tetragon.io/docs/concepts/tracing-policy/hooks/)

### `CONFIG_KPROBE_EVENTS`
Exposes kprobe attachment through the **perf/trace event API** (as opposed to the ftrace text interface). `BPF_PROG_TYPE_KPROBE` and `BPF_PROG_TYPE_KRETPROBE` programs are attached via this interface.
- [Kernel docs: kprobe-event](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/trace/kprobetrace.html)

### `CONFIG_UPROBES`
Enables **user-space probes** — breakpoints inserted into ELF binaries at specific offsets, mapped into process memory. OpenTelemetry OBI uses uprobes to auto-instrument language runtimes (Go, Python, Node.js, Java, Rust) for distributed tracing without modifying application code. Unlike kprobes (which hook the kernel), uprobes hook into userspace processes.
- [Kernel docs: uprobes](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/trace/uprobetracer.html)
- [OpenTelemetry eBPF Instrumentation (OBI)](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/zero-code/obi/)
- [Using eBPF with OpenTelemetry: Zero-Code Auto-Instrumentation](https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2025-12-10-ebpf-with-opentelemetry-auto-instrumentation/view)

### `CONFIG_UPROBE_EVENTS`
The perf-event interface layer for uprobes; analogous to `CONFIG_KPROBE_EVENTS` but for userspace targets. Required for `BPF_PROG_TYPE_KPROBE` programs attached to uprobes. Enables functions like `bpf_get_current_pid_tgid()` and map operations to work correctly in uprobe context.
- [Kernel docs: uprobe-event](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/trace/uprobetracer.html)

### `CONFIG_TRACEPOINTS`
Defines the **static tracepoint instrumentation framework** — pre-placed hooks in the kernel (scheduler, memory, networking subsystems) with stable ABIs. Used by Tetragon (`sched_process_exec`, etc.) and OBI.
- [Kernel docs: tracepoints](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/trace/tracepoints.html)

### `CONFIG_PERF_EVENTS`
The **perf subsystem** — hardware performance counters, software events, and the ring-buffer transport used by BPF programs to send data to userspace. All `perf_event_open`-based BPF attachment (kprobes, uprobes, tracepoints) depends on this.
- [Kernel docs: perf events](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/admin-guide/perf-security.html)

---

## 5 · tc-BPF — Cilium datapath

> Cilium's primary datapath attaches BPF programs at the **Traffic Control (tc)** layer on each veth/pod interface to implement load balancing, policy enforcement, and encapsulation without going through iptables. This is the **fast path** that processes every packet in the kernel. See [Cilium datapath architecture](https://docs.cilium.io/en/stable/network/ebpf/index.html) and [technical deep dives](https://medium.com/codex/cilium-technical-deep-dive-understanding-the-ebpf-data-path-2b942e3150ed) for implementation details.

### `CONFIG_NET_SCHED`
The **Queueing Discipline (qdisc) framework** — the scheduling and classification layer that sits between the network stack and device drivers. tc-BPF programs execute here at ingress and egress, making it the optimal hook for network policy and load balancing.
- [Kernel docs: tc](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/networking/net_sched.html)
- [How to Deploy Cilium CNI for eBPF-Powered Kubernetes Networking](https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-01-07-ebpf-cilium-kubernetes-networking/view)

### `CONFIG_NET_SCH_INGRESS`
Enables the **clsact / ingress qdisc**, which is where Cilium hooks `BPF_PROG_TYPE_SCHED_CLS` programs on the *ingress* path (packets arriving at a veth before the network stack processes them). Without this, tc ingress BPF cannot be attached.
- [Cilium datapath](https://docs.cilium.io/en/stable/network/ebpf/intro/)

### `CONFIG_NET_CLS_ACT`
Enables **classifier-action chaining** within tc, allowing classifiers (like `cls_bpf`) to invoke actions (like `act_bpf` or `act_mirred`). Cilium's tc programs act both as classifier and action, making this option essential for its operation.
- [Kernel docs: tc actions](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/networking/net_sched.html)

### `CONFIG_NET_CLS_BPF`
The **`cls_bpf` classifier** — loads a BPF program as a tc classifier. This is the primary mechanism Cilium uses to attach eBPF programs to tc hooks on host and pod interfaces.
- [Cilium BPF and XDP reference](https://docs.cilium.io/en/stable/network/ebpf/intro/)
- [BPF Architecture — Cilium documentation](https://docs.cilium.io/en/latest/reference-guides/bpf/architecture/)

### `CONFIG_NET_ACT_BPF`
The **`act_bpf` action** — allows a BPF program to be invoked as a tc action (distinct from a classifier). Some Cilium and Tetragon configurations use this for supplementary actions.
- [Kernel docs: tc BPF](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/networking/net_sched.html)

### `CONFIG_NET_ACT_MIRRED`
The **`act_mirred` action** — redirects or mirrors packets between interfaces at the tc layer. Cilium uses this to steer traffic from host interfaces into container namespaces and vice versa, enabling pod-to-node and node-to-pod packet steering.
- [man8: tc-mirred](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/tc-mirred.8.html)
- [Container Networking Deep Dive](https://blog.shellnetsecurity.com/posts/2025/container-networking-fundamentals/)

---

## 6 · LWT-BPF — Cilium host routing / IPv6

> **Lightweight Tunnels (LWT)** allow custom packet transformations to be associated with routing table entries. Cilium uses LWT-BPF for host-routing and encapsulation decisions on specific routes.

### `CONFIG_LWTUNNEL`
The **LWT framework** core. Provides the hooks (input, output, xmit) that BPF and other encapsulation modules register handlers for within the routing layer.
- [Kernel docs: LWT](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/networking/lwtunnel.html)

### `CONFIG_LWTUNNEL_BPF`
Enables **BPF programs as LWT hooks**. Cilium uses `lwt_xmit` BPF programs to handle encapsulation (VXLAN/Geneve) for specific routing table entries, enabling per-route eBPF processing without tc.
- [Cilium routing](https://docs.cilium.io/en/stable/network/concepts/routing/)

---

## 7 · Cgroup controllers — Docker, Tetragon process correlation

> cgroup v2 is the unified hierarchy used by Docker (with systemd cgroup driver) and Kubernetes. Tetragon reads cgroup identity to correlate kernel events with pods/containers.

### `CONFIG_CGROUPS`
The **cgroup subsystem core**. Required by every container runtime and by Tetragon for process tree tracking.
- [Kernel docs: cgroup v2](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.html)

### `CONFIG_MEMCG`
**Memory cgroup controller** — enforces per-container memory limits and provides OOM tracking. Docker's `--memory` flag and Kubernetes resource limits both depend on this.
- [Kernel docs: memory cgroup](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.html#memory)

### `CONFIG_BLK_CGROUP`
**Block I/O cgroup controller** — enables per-container I/O throttling (used by Docker's `blkio` settings and the newer `io` cgroup v2 controller).
- [Kernel docs: io cgroup](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.html#io)

### `CONFIG_CGROUP_PIDS`
**PID cgroup controller** — limits the number of processes a container can create, preventing fork bombs. Required by Docker's `--pids-limit`.
- [Kernel docs: pids cgroup](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.html#pid)

### `CONFIG_CGROUP_FREEZER`
**Freezer cgroup controller** — allows a container's processes to be paused/resumed atomically. Used by Docker checkpoint/restore (CRIU) and some orchestrators.
This option controls the legacy cgroup v1 freezer controller; cgroup v2's
`cgroup.freeze` mechanism does not require this legacy option.
- [Kernel docs: cgroup freezer](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.html)

### `CONFIG_CGROUP_DEVICE`
**Device cgroup controller** — allows/denies access to specific device nodes within a container (used to implement Docker's device whitelist and Kubernetes `allowedDevices`).
This option supplies the legacy cgroup v1 device controller. On cgroup v2,
device access is controlled through cgroup BPF programs (`CONFIG_CGROUP_BPF`).
- [Kernel docs: device cgroup](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.html#device-controller)

### `CONFIG_CGROUP_SCHED`
**CPU cgroup controller** — enforces CPU shares, quotas (`cpu.max`), and real-time scheduling limits per cgroup. Required for Docker `--cpus` and Kubernetes CPU requests/limits.
- [Kernel docs: cpu cgroup](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.html#cpu)

### `CONFIG_SOCK_CGROUP_DATA`
Embeds **cgroup identity into socket structures** so BPF programs can read `sk->cgroup` directly. This is how Cilium and OBI associate a network connection with the pod/container that owns it, without an expensive cgroup lookup per packet.
- [Kernel docs: cgroup BPF](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/bpf/index.html)

---

## 8 · Netfilter / iptables / conntrack

> Cilium can run in pure eBPF mode (no iptables) but ships compatibility shims; Docker's network plumbing always uses iptables/netfilter. Tetragon reads conntrack to correlate network events.

### `CONFIG_NETFILTER`
The **Netfilter framework** — the hook-based packet filtering layer that iptables, nftables, and conntrack all live on.
- [Netfilter project](https://www.netfilter.org/)

### `CONFIG_NETFILTER_ADVANCED`
Unlocks **advanced Netfilter features** (set matching, ipset, newer match/target modules). Required to compile in `NETFILTER_XT_*` modules below.
- [Netfilter project](https://www.netfilter.org/)

### `CONFIG_NF_CONNTRACK`
The **connection tracking subsystem** — maintains state tables for TCP/UDP/ICMP sessions. Docker MASQUERADE, Cilium NAT, and Tetragon network-event enrichment all depend on conntrack.
- [Kernel docs: conntrack](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/networking/nf_conntrack-sysctl.html)

### `CONFIG_NF_NAT`
The **NAT engine** built on top of conntrack. Docker uses MASQUERADE for container egress NAT; Cilium uses it in iptables-compatibility mode.
- [Netfilter NAT documentation](https://www.netfilter.org/documentation/)

### `CONFIG_NF_TABLES`
The **nftables framework** — the modern, set-based replacement for iptables. Required by newer Docker versions that default to nftables as the backend, and by Kubernetes clusters using the nftables kube-proxy mode.
- [nftables wiki](https://wiki.nftables.org/)

### `CONFIG_NF_TABLES_INET`
The **inet (dual IPv4/IPv6) nftables family** — allows writing a single nftables ruleset that applies to both IP versions, which is how Docker and Cilium use it.
- [nftables wiki](https://wiki.nftables.org/)

### `CONFIG_IP_NF_IPTABLES`
The **iptables framework for IPv4** — the classic packet filter table architecture.
- [iptables man page](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/iptables.8.html)

### `CONFIG_IP_NF_FILTER`
The **`filter` table** for iptables (`INPUT`, `OUTPUT`, `FORWARD` chains). Docker and kube-proxy write FORWARD rules here.
- [iptables man page](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/iptables.8.html)

### `CONFIG_IP_NF_NAT`
The **`nat` table** for iptables (`PREROUTING`, `POSTROUTING` chains). Docker's container MASQUERADE and port publishing rules live here.
- [iptables man page](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/iptables.8.html)

### `CONFIG_IP_NF_MANGLE`
The **`mangle` table** for iptables — used for packet marking and TTL manipulation. Cilium (iptables mode) uses marks to identify traffic that has already been processed by BPF.
- [iptables man page](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/iptables.8.html)

### `CONFIG_IP6_NF_IPTABLES`
The **ip6tables framework** — IPv6 equivalent of `CONFIG_IP_NF_IPTABLES`.
- [ip6tables man page](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/ip6tables.8.html)

### `CONFIG_IP6_NF_FILTER`
The IPv6 **`filter` table** for ip6tables.
- [ip6tables man page](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/ip6tables.8.html)

### `CONFIG_IP6_NF_NAT`
The IPv6 **`nat` table** for ip6tables — required for IPv6 NAT (NPTv6, masquerade in IPv6-only setups).
- [ip6tables man page](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/ip6tables.8.html)

### `CONFIG_NETFILTER_XT_MARK`
The **`mark` xtables match/target** — sets or matches the `skb->mark` field on packets. Cilium uses marks heavily in iptables mode to steer traffic and avoid double-NAT.
- [iptables-extensions: mark](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/iptables-extensions.8.html)

### `CONFIG_NETFILTER_XT_MATCH_BPF`
The **`bpf` xtables match** — runs a classic BPF filter on a packet as an iptables match condition. Allows existing iptables rules to delegate classification to a BPF program.
- [iptables-extensions: bpf](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/iptables-extensions.8.html)

### `CONFIG_NETFILTER_XT_MATCH_SOCKET`
The **`socket` xtables match** — looks up the socket that would receive the packet. Used by Cilium and Envoy to identify locally-owned connections for transparent proxy rules.
- [iptables-extensions: socket](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/iptables-extensions.8.html)

### `CONFIG_NETFILTER_XT_TARGET_TPROXY`
The **TPROXY xtables target** — redirects a packet to a local socket without changing its destination IP/port, enabling **transparent proxying**. Envoy relies on TPROXY to intercept traffic without `SO_REUSEPORT` tricks.
- [iptables-extensions: TPROXY](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/iptables-extensions.8.html)
- [Envoy transparent proxy](https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/configuration/listeners/lis_filters/original_dst_filter)

### `CONFIG_NETFILTER_XT_TARGET_CT`
The **`CT` xtables target** — allows explicit manipulation of conntrack entries (set zone, helper, status flags). Used by some Cilium configurations to assign conntrack zones per interface.
It depends on `IP_NF_RAW || IP6_NF_RAW`. This profile sets both raw-table
options to `y` so Kconfig can keep the requested CT target built in.
- [iptables-extensions: CT](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/iptables-extensions.8.html)

### `CONFIG_IP_NF_RAW` / `CONFIG_IP6_NF_RAW`
Enable the IPv4 and IPv6 raw tables for rules evaluated before normal connection
tracking. These supply the parent dependency for the built-in CT target and are
also used by NOTRACK/TRACE configurations.

---

## 9 · Virtual netdevs — container networking + Cilium overlays

> Container networking is built on virtual network devices that connect namespaces and interfaces. Understanding these is essential for debugging container connectivity issues. See [container networking deep dives](https://blog.shellnetsecurity.com/posts/2025/container-networking-fundamentals/) and [advanced Linux networking techniques](https://blog.shellnetsecurity.com/posts/2025/advanced-linux-networking-techniques/) for comprehensive explanations.

### `CONFIG_TUN`
The **TUN/TAP driver** — creates virtual point-to-point (TUN) or Ethernet (TAP) devices. Used by WireGuard's userspace fallback, some VPN clients, and QEMU/KVM inside WSL2.
- [Kernel docs: tuntap](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/networking/tuntap.html)

### `CONFIG_VETH`
**Virtual Ethernet pairs** — the fundamental building block of container networking. Every Docker/Kubernetes container gets a `veth` pair: one end in the container namespace, the other on the host where Cilium attaches tc-BPF programs. Each veth acts as a bidirectional pipe between two network namespaces.
- [man8: ip-link veth](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/ip-link.8.html)
- [UMA Technology: Network Configurations for Kubernetes pods](https://umatechnology.org/network-configurations-for-kubernetes-pods-built-on-linux/)

### `CONFIG_BRIDGE`
The **software bridge driver** — the Linux equivalent of a network switch. Docker's default `bridge` network mode puts containers behind a `docker0` bridge that forwards traffic between the container and host network namespaces.
- [Kernel docs: bridge](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/networking/bridge.html)
- [Container Networking Deep Dive: Bridge, Host, and Overlay](https://dasroot.net/posts/2026/03/container-networking-deep-dive-bridge-host-overlay/)

### `CONFIG_BRIDGE_VLAN_FILTERING`
Enables **VLAN filtering on bridges** — allows per-port VLAN membership, used by more advanced CNI plugins and multi-tenant Docker setups.
- [Kernel docs: bridge](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/networking/bridge.html)

### `CONFIG_VXLAN`
The **VXLAN encapsulation driver** — encapsulates L2 frames in UDP datagrams to create overlay networks across L3 boundaries. Cilium's default overlay mode in many deployments. Provides multi-node pod connectivity by tunneling packets through UDP over the host network.
- [RFC 7348: VXLAN](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7348)
- [Cilium VXLAN overlay](https://docs.cilium.io/en/stable/network/concepts/routing/#vxlan-based-multi-node-pod-connectivity)
- [GitHub: tunnel-cni VXLAN/Geneve backend](https://github.com/ebpf-networking/tunnel-cni)

### `CONFIG_GENEVE`
The **Geneve encapsulation driver** — a more flexible overlay encapsulation than VXLAN, with extensible TLV options for metadata. Cilium supports Geneve as an alternative overlay; OVN also uses it.
- [RFC 8926: Geneve](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8926)
- [Capturing Network Traffic Over Cilium VTEP Tunnels with eBPF](https://engineering.01cloud.com/2026/01/26/capturing-network-traffic-over-cilium-vtep-tunnels-with-ebpf-a-practical-guide/)

### `CONFIG_MACVLAN`
**MAC VLAN** — creates virtual interfaces that share the same physical NIC but have distinct MAC addresses and can be placed in separate namespaces. Used by some CNI plugins and Docker `macvlan` network mode.
- [Kernel docs: macvlan](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/networking/net_dev_ctx.html)

### `CONFIG_IPVLAN`
**IP VLAN** — like MACVLAN but shares the parent's MAC; only IP addresses differ. Used by `ipvlan`-mode CNI plugins and some Cilium routing configurations.
- [Kernel docs: ipvlan](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/networking/ipvlan.html)

### `CONFIG_DUMMY`
The **dummy network interface driver** — a virtual interface that swallows all traffic (like loopback but without the loopback semantics). Cilium uses dummy interfaces as attachment points for host-facing BPF programs.
- [man8: ip-link dummy](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/ip-link.8.html)

### `CONFIG_IFB`
**Intermediate Functional Block** — a virtual device used to redirect ingress traffic to an egress queue so that standard tc qdiscs (which only work egress) can be applied to incoming traffic. Used in some bandwidth-shaping setups alongside Cilium.
- [man8: tc-ifb](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/tc-ifb.8.html)

---

## 10 · Crypto / IPsec / WireGuard — Cilium transparent encryption

### `CONFIG_XFRM`
The **IPsec/XFRM framework** — the kernel's transform layer for encrypting and authenticating IP packets. Cilium's IPsec transparent encryption (node-to-node) runs through XFRM.
- [Kernel docs: XFRM](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/networking/xfrm_device.html)
- [Cilium IPsec](https://docs.cilium.io/en/stable/network/encryption-ipsec/)

### `CONFIG_XFRM_USER`
The **Netlink interface to XFRM** — exposes XFRM policy and SA management to userspace daemons (strongSwan, Cilium's IPsec operator) via `AF_KEY`/`XFRM_MSG_*`.
- [Kernel docs: XFRM](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/networking/xfrm_device.html)

### `CONFIG_XFRM_ALGO`
The **algorithm module framework for XFRM** — allows cipher and hash modules (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305, SHA-256, etc.) to be registered and used by ESP/AH.
- [Kernel docs: XFRM](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/networking/xfrm_device.html)

### `CONFIG_INET_ESP`
**ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload) for IPv4** — the IPsec encapsulation protocol that provides encryption + authentication. Cilium IPsec mode uses ESP between nodes.
- [RFC 4303: ESP](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4303)

### `CONFIG_INET6_ESP`
**ESP for IPv6** — the IPv6 equivalent of `CONFIG_INET_ESP`.
- [RFC 4303: ESP](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4303)

### `CONFIG_WIREGUARD`
The **WireGuard VPN module** — a modern, high-performance, cryptographically opinionated VPN built into the kernel. Cilium uses WireGuard as its alternative transparent encryption mode (simpler key management than IPsec).
- [WireGuard project](https://www.wireguard.com/)
- [Cilium WireGuard](https://docs.cilium.io/en/stable/network/encryption-wireguard/)

---

## 11 · Storage — Docker overlay2 + alternate drivers

### `CONFIG_OVERLAY_FS`
The **OverlayFS union filesystem** — the default Docker storage driver (`overlay2`). Stacks a read-only image layer with a per-container read-write layer, enabling copy-on-write semantics for container image layers.
- [Kernel docs: overlayfs](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/filesystems/overlayfs.html)
- [Docker overlay2 driver](https://docs.docker.com/storage/storagedriver/overlayfs-driver/)

### `CONFIG_FUSE_FS`
The **FUSE (Filesystem in Userspace) driver** — allows filesystems to be implemented in userspace. Used by some container image formats (Nydus, SOCI snapshotter), rootless container storage drivers, and development tooling inside WSL2.
- [Kernel docs: FUSE](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/filesystems/fuse.html)

---

## 12 · Security primitives — required by Docker/runc, Tetragon, BPF-LSM

> These options provide kernel-level security mechanisms used by container runtimes and security agents. See [Linux Observability with BPF](https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/linux-observability-with/9781492050193/ch08.html) and [LSM BPF documentation](https://docs.kernel.org/bpf/prog_lsm.html) for comprehensive coverage.

### `CONFIG_SECCOMP`
The **secure computing mode** framework — allows a process to restrict its own (or a child's) allowed syscalls to a whitelist. Docker and runc apply seccomp profiles to every container; Tetragon's BPF-LSM mode can also leverage it. This is the **default container sandbox mechanism**.
- [Kernel docs: seccomp](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/userspace-api/seccomp_filter.html)
- [Docker seccomp profile](https://docs.docker.com/engine/security/seccomp/)
- [Seccomp BPF documentation](https://docs.kernel.org/userspace-api/seccomp_filter.html)

### `CONFIG_SECCOMP_FILTER`
Enables the **BPF-based seccomp filter** mechanism (as opposed to the older SECCOMP_MODE_STRICT). This is what `docker run --security-opt seccomp=profile.json` uses. Filters are evaluated as BPF bytecode at syscall entry, enabling fine-grained per-syscall argument filtering.
- [Kernel docs: seccomp_filter](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/userspace-api/seccomp_filter.html)
- [Practical Guide to Linux Security with Seccomp](https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/linux-observability-with/9781492050193/ch08.html)

### `CONFIG_AUDIT`
The **Linux Audit subsystem** — logs security-relevant events (syscalls, file accesses, policy decisions) to a ring buffer readable by `auditd`. Required by many container security benchmarks (CIS Docker Benchmark) and by SELinux/AppArmor policy enforcement logging. Essential for compliance and forensics.
- [Kernel docs: audit](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/admin-guide/audit.html)
- [Kernel runtime security instrumentation (LWN)](https://lwn.net/Articles/798157/)

---

## 13 · Misc performance / observability

### `CONFIG_TRANSPARENT_HUGEPAGE`
Enables **Transparent Huge Pages (THP)** — the kernel automatically promotes 4 KiB page mappings to 2 MiB huge pages when possible. Reduces TLB pressure for large working sets (JVM heaps, Envoy proxy buffers, BPF map backing memory).
- [Kernel docs: THP](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/admin-guide/mm/transhuge.html)

### `CONFIG_HUGETLBFS`
Provides the **HugeTLB filesystem** — allows applications to explicitly `mmap` pre-allocated huge pages (1 GiB on x86). Used by performance-sensitive databases and DPDK-style packet processing.
- [Kernel docs: hugetlbpage](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/admin-guide/mm/hugetlbpage.html)

### `CONFIG_IKCONFIG`
Embeds the **full kernel config** into the kernel binary itself. Allows any tool running on the system to read the config without needing access to the build tree.
- [Kconfig: CONFIG_IKCONFIG](https://cateee.net/lkddb/web-lkddb/IKCONFIG.html)

### `CONFIG_IKCONFIG_PROC`
Exposes the embedded config via **`/proc/config.gz`**. Tools like `cilium-bugtool`, `tetra`, and `bpftool feature` read this to verify kernel capabilities at runtime.
- [Kconfig: CONFIG_IKCONFIG_PROC](https://cateee.net/lkddb/web-lkddb/IKCONFIG_PROC.html)

### `CONFIG_IKHEADERS`
Embeds kernel headers in `/sys/kernel/kheaders.tar.xz` for tools that compile
against the running kernel. BPF CO-RE normally relies on BTF and does not require
this archive. Header availability also does not supply a compiler or LLVM tools.
- [Kconfig: CONFIG_IKHEADERS](https://cateee.net/lkddb/web-lkddb/IKHEADERS.html)

### `CONFIG_LOCALVERSION`
Adds `-microsoft-standard-WSL2-ebpf` to the kernel release so the custom profile
can be distinguished from a stock kernel. The runtime check compares the full
release with `kernel-release.txt` recorded during the build.

## Enforcement additions

### `CONFIG_FUNCTION_ERROR_INJECTION`
Enables error injection into kernel functions annotated with
`ALLOW_ERROR_INJECTION()`. It is a dependency of `CONFIG_BPF_KPROBE_OVERRIDE`.

### `CONFIG_BPF_KPROBE_OVERRIDE`
Allows BPF programs to override the return value of eligible kprobed functions.
Tetragon's kprobe `Override` action needs this option. It does not make arbitrary
kernel functions overridable, and ordinary tracing does not require it.
Validate the capability with `sudo tetra probe`, then test the actual policy.
- [Tetragon Override action](https://tetragon.io/docs/concepts/tracing-policy/selectors/)

---

- [RFC 8926: Geneve](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8926) — Generic Network Virtualization Encapsulation
- [RFC 4303: IPsec ESP](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4303) — Encapsulating Security Payload
- [WireGuard White Paper](https://www.wireguard.com/papers/wireguard.pdf) — Modern cryptographic VPN design
- [nftables Wiki](https://wiki.nftables.org/) — Modern iptables replacement

### Tools & Practical Guides
- [eBPF Based Container Networking Performance Comparison — TNO/OS3](https://rp.os3.nl/2016-2017/p84/presentation.pdf) — Network performance analysis
- [GitHub: tunnel-cni](https://github.com/ebpf-networking/tunnel-cni) — VXLAN/Geneve CNI plugin
- [Capturing Traffic Over Cilium VTEP Tunnels with eBPF — 01cloud](https://engineering.01cloud.com/2026/01/26/capturing-network-traffic-over-cilium-vtep-tunnels-with-ebpf-a-practical-guide/) — Practical packet capture guide
- [Envoy Original Destination Filter](https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/configuration/listeners/lis_filters/original_dst_filter) — Transparent proxy configuration
